claim: PlxnA1Y1815F mutation in mice recapitulates PlxnA1-/- recrossing phenotype but not stalling phenotype.
source: Interestingly, while no difference of stalling was observed between PlxnA1+/+ and PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F embryos, the recrossing cases were exclusively associated with loss of one or two PlxnA1 gene copies, recapitulating PlxnA1-/- embryos phenotype (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from DiI labeling of commissural tracts in mouse embryos, showing quantitative analysis of phenotypes across different genotypes.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F expressing axons display tortuous trajectories during floor plate navigation.
source: Moreover, in the Y1815F context, axon trajectories appeared disorganized, with axons baring a tortuous aspect, even when they could achieve FP crossing (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images showing axon trajectories in PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F embryos compared to wild-type.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F mutation does not affect pre-crossing commissural navigation.
source: Their pattern revealed no obvious defects of coursing toward the FP, indicating that PlxnA1 Y1815 residue is dispensable for the pre-crossing navigation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data of transverse sections showing Robo3 and L1CAM markers in E12.5 embryos.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F mutation is consistent with previous findings that PlxnA1 is not delivered at the growth cone surface prior to FP entry.
source: This is consistent with our previous finding that PlxnA1 is not delivered at the growth cone surface prior to the FP entry, thus having no expected pre-crossing role (Pignata et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Pignata et al., 2019) to support the interpretation of current findings.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F mutation does not prevent PlxnA1 synthesis or trafficking to axons.
source: Thus, the Y1815 mutation does not prevent PlxnA1 synthesis nor its trafficking to the axon.
evidence: The claim is based on PlxnA1 expression analysis showing similar expression levels between WT and PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F embryos.

claim: The ability of commissural axons to maintain a straight trajectory toward the FP exit requires functional PlxnA1-SlitC signaling.
source: Thus, the ability of commissural axons to maintain a straight trajectory toward the FP exit requires a functional PlxnA1-SlitC signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PlxnA1Y1815F mutation, which disrupts SlitC signaling, results in disorganized axon trajectories.

claim: PlxnA1-Nrp2-Sema3B signaling remains sufficient for pushing commissural axons toward the FP exit in the absence of PlxnA1-SlitC signaling.
source: In contrast, the lack of stalling phenotype in PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F embryos indicates that the guidance forces resulting from the unaffected PlxnA1-Nrp2-Sema3B signaling remain sufficient for pushing commissural axons toward the FP exit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of stalling phenotype in PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F embryos despite the presence of recrossing defects.

claim: Re-expressing PlxnA1Y1815F in PlxnA1-/- embryos results in decreased straight trajectories (54%) compared to PlxnA1WT (86%).
source: Interestingly, the proportion of straight trajectory decreased from 86% in the WT condition to 54% in the PlxnA1Y1815F one.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon trajectories in electroporated PlxnA1-/- mouse open-books.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F expressing axons show increased deviations (20%) compared to PlxnA1WT (9%).
source: Conversely, we observed significant increase of deviations (from 9% to 20%) and premature turns (from 5% to 27%) for pHluo-PlxnA1Y1815F+ axons compared to pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ ones (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon behaviors in electroporated mouse open-books.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F expressing axons show increased premature turns (27%) compared to PlxnA1WT (5%).
source: Conversely, we observed significant increase of deviations (from 9% to 20%) and premature turns (from 5% to 27%) for pHluo-PlxnA1Y1815F+ axons compared to pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ ones (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon behaviors in electroporated mouse open-books.

claim: PlxnA1WT+ growth cones exhibit 73% straight trajectories while PlxnA1Y1815F+ ones only 36%.
source: Interestingly, pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ growth cones exhibited 73% of straight trajectories while PlxnA1Y1815F ones only 36%.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of individual axon trajectories in mouse open-books.

claim: In chicken embryos, 63% of PlxnA1WT axons had straight trajectories compared to only 34% for PlxnA1Y1815F.
source: We found that 63% of axons had a straight trajectory in the PlxnA1WT condition, for only 34% in the PlxnA1Y1815F condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse analysis of commissural axon navigation in electroporated chicken embryos.

claim: 36% of PlxnA1Y1815F axons were tortuous compared to only 17% for PlxnA1WT in chicken embryos.
source: Conversely, 36% of PlxnA1Y1815F axons were tortuous, for only 17% for the PlxnA1WT ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse analysis of commissural axon navigation in electroporated chicken embryos.

claim: The proportion of early turns increased from 11% to 19% in the PlxnA1Y1815F condition compared to PlxnA1WT in chicken embryos.
source: Moreover, the proportion of early turns increased from 11% to 19% in the PlxnA1Y1815F condition compared to the PlxnA1WT one (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse analysis of commissural axon navigation in electroporated chicken embryos.

claim: The rate of growth cone stalling was comparable between PlxnA1WT (9%) and PlxnA1Y1815F (10%) conditions in chicken embryos.
source: The rate of growth cone stalling was comparable in both conditions (9% and 10% for PlxnA1WT and PlxnA1Y1815F respectively), which was also consistent with the lack of increased stalling phenotype in PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F mouse embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse analysis in chicken embryos and is consistent with mouse embryo data.

claim: The percentage of straight trajectories significantly decreased from 83% in PlxnA1WT to 53% in PlxnA1Y1815F in chicken embryos.
source: As in mouse open-books, we found the percentage of straight trajectories significantly decreased from 83% in the PlxnA1WT condition to 53% in the PlxnA1Y1815F one, with correlated increase in curved shapes (Figure 2H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of axon trajectory curvatures in chicken embryos.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F receptor occupies a much larger membrane domain, overflowing into the adjacent axon shaft compartment, compared to PlxnA1WT which is mostly restricted to the growth cone.
source: However, while PlxnA1WT was mostly restricted to the growth cone, PlxnA1Y1815F occupied a much larger membrane domain, overflowing in the adjacent axon shaft compartment (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging of pHluo-receptor distribution in PlxnA1-/- mouse open-books.

claim: Y1815 mutation alters PlxnA1 cell surface pattern in navigating commissural axons.
source: Thus, the Y1815 mutation alters PlxnA1 cell surface pattern in navigating commissural axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PlxnA1Y1815F has a different membrane distribution pattern compared to PlxnA1WT.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F/+ embryos have a recrossing phenotype while PlxnA1+/- ones do not.
source: Our previous and present analyses indicate that PlxnA1Y1815F/+ embryos have a recrossing phenotype while PlxnA1+/- ones do not (Delloye-Bourgeois et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by current data and references a previous publication (Delloye-Bourgeois et al., 2015).

claim: Nearly 100% of growth cones navigating the FP had sorted PlxnA1 receptor before midline crossing in both PlxnA1WT and PlxnA1Y1815F conditions.
source: Interestingly, in both PlxnA1WT and PlxnA1Y1815F conditions, nearly 100% of the growth cones navigating the FP had sorted the receptor before midline crossing, indicating that the temporal pattern of membrane insertion within the FP was unaffected by the Y1815 mutation (Figure 3C and D and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by video-microscopy analysis of pHluo-receptor dynamics in chicken open-books.

claim: A significant proportion of PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones sorted the receptor prior to FP entry.
source: Nevertheless, we also observed that a significant proportion of PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones, which could navigate the FP, had sorted the receptor prior to the FP entry (Figure 3C and Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by video-microscopy observations in chicken open-books.

claim: PlxnA1WT membrane pool concentrates at the front of growth cones navigating the FP.
source: We recently reported using Atto-647N-conjugated green fluorescent protein (GFP) nanobodies and STED microscopy that the membrane pool of PlxnA1WT concentrates at the front of growth cones navigating the FP (Pignata et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Pignata et al., 2019) to provide context for current findings.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F distribution spans from the front to the rear of the growth cone, in contrast to PlxnA1WT.
source: Notably, in sharp contrast with our observations of PlxnA1WT, PlxnA1Y1815F spanned from the front to the rear of the growth cone (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by STED microscopy imaging of receptor distribution in growth cones.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F spatial distribution in commissural axons navigating the FP is altered, revealing that the mutation might interfere with SlitC-specific traffic and signaling.
source: Thus, PlxnA1Y1815F spatial distribution in commissural axons navigating the FP is altered, which reveals that the mutation might interfere with SlitC-specific traffic and signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in receptor distribution patterns between WT and mutant forms.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F has faster membrane diffusion than PlxnA1WT.
source: Thus, PlxnA1Y1815F has a faster membrane diffusion than PlxnA1WT.
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP experiments showing faster fluorescence recovery for PlxnA1Y1815F.

claim: Exocytosis events might be unaffected by the Y1815F mutation.
source: The stability of the difference over time also suggests that exocytosis events might be unaffected by the mutation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments.

claim: Y1815F mutation results in relapse of PlxnA1 mobility at the cell membrane which could affect the ability of the receptor to mediate SlitC signal.
source: Thus, Y1815F mutation results in relapse of PlxnA1 mobility at the cell membrane which, either upstream or downstream of SlitC binding, could affect the ability of the receptor to mediate SlitC signal.
evidence: The claim is inferred from FRAP data showing increased membrane mobility of the mutant receptor.

claim: FP glia cells have a typical progenitor-like bipolar morphology with a dorsal apical anchor at the lumen of the central canal and a basal process laying ventrally on the basal lamina.
source: Glial cells, composing the FP, have a typical progenitor-like bipolar morphology, with a dorsal apical anchor at the lumen of the central canal and a basal process laying ventrally on the basal lamina, even though some studies suggested these cells have complex morphology (Campbell and Peterson, 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about FP glia morphology and cites a previous study (Campbell and Peterson, 1993).

claim: BEN staining revealed a dense network of processes in the basal compartment corresponding to the axon path, with BEN+ structures aligned in the left-right axis.
source: The staining revealed a dense network of processes in the basal compartment corresponding to the axon path, in particular with BEN+ structures aligned in the left–right axis (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data of E4 chick embryo transverse sections.

claim: The basal process of FP glial cells is not a simple extension but rather is a ramified structure.
source: We observed that the basal process of the glial cell is not a simple extension but rather is a ramified structure (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by sparse electroporation and imaging of individual FP cells in chick embryos.

claim: 3D reconstruction revealed FP glial cells have a 'squid-like' structure with a basal process subdivided into several pillars, with typically several anchors to the ventral pole.
source: 3D reconstruction with IMARIS software after deconvolution treatment of the images revealed a 'squid-like' structure, with a basal process subdivided into several pillars, with typically several anchors to the ventral pole (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction analysis of confocal microscopy images.

claim: FP glial cell pillars are much larger in the left-right axis than in the rostro-caudal axis.
source: The pillars appeared much larger in the left–right axis than in the rostro-caudal one, as suggested by previous data from electronic microscopy (Okabe et al., 2004; Figure 4E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by current imaging data and references previous electron microscopy studies (Okabe et al., 2004).

claim: Commissural growth cones are individually intercalated between glial cell processes.
source: We observed that commissural growth cones are individually intercalated between glial cell processes (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging of Math1-mbTomato electroporated axons with BEN immunostaining.

claim: Commissural growth cones have an oblong shape, flattened in the left-right dimension and elongated in the dorso-ventral dimension.
source: We observed them infiltrating the space between pillars, having an oblong shape, flattened in the left–right dimension and elongated in the dorso-ventral one (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by 3D reconstruction of growth cone morphology from confocal images.

claim: FP glia elaborate highly complex mesh of basal processes whose stereotypic spatial organization provides a physical frame for commissural growth cones, likely imposing numerous and repeated contacts all over the FP navigation.
source: Thus, FP glia elaborate highly complex mesh of basal processes whose stereotypic spatial organization provides a physical frame for commissural growth cones, likely imposing numerous and repeated contacts all over the FP navigation (Figure 4K and Videos 9–12).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed complex architecture of FP glia basal processes and their spatial relationship with navigating axons.

claim: Sema3B-GFP protein clusters distribute evenly in the FP, arranged in columns reflecting their localization along the basal processes.
source: Quantitative analysis of the GFP distribution revealed that protein clusters distributed evenly in the FP, arranged in columns reflecting their localization along the basal processes.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of Sema3B-GFP knock-in mouse transverse sections.

claim: Glial cells display massive white staining in their apical part, reflecting the presence of uncleaved Slit2-FL and/or overlapping Slit2N and Slit2C fragments.
source: We observed that glial cells display a massive white staining in their apical part, reflecting the presence of the uncleaved Slit2-FL and/or overlapping Slit2N and Slit2C fragments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of overlapping Cerulean and Venus fluorescence in the apical compartment of electroporated FP cells.

claim: The basal compartments show higher degree of separation of Slit2 fragments compared to the apical compartment.
source: Conversely, the basal compartments, in particular the most ventral one in which commissural axons preferentially path, showed higher degree of separation of the Slit2 fragments, as quantified by a Pearson coefficient evaluation (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pearson coefficient analysis of dual-tagged Slit2 fluorescence in different FP compartments.

claim: Both Slit2N and Slit2C fragments have a graded pattern with higher levels in the basal a versus basal b compartment.
source: Analysis of Cerulean (Slit2N) and Venus (Slit2C) fluorescence showed that both Slit2 fragments had a graded pattern, with higher levels in the basal a versus basal b compartment.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity in different FP compartments.

claim: Slit2C is significantly enriched in the basal b compartment when compared to Slit2N.
source: Yet, Slit2C was significantly enriched in the basal b compartment, when compared to Slit2N (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of Slit2N and Slit2C fluorescence intensity ratios.

claim: Slit2N displays similar distributions whether issued from endogenous processing or expressed individually.
source: Interestingly, whereas Slit2N displayed similar distributions, Slit2C diffused massively in the axon path when issued from Slit2 cleavage (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Slit2N distribution from dual-tagged construct versus isolated fragment expression.

claim: Slit2C diffuses massively in the axon path when issued from Slit2 cleavage compared to when expressed as an isolated fragment.
source: Interestingly, whereas Slit2N displayed similar distributions, Slit2C diffused massively in the axon path when issued from Slit2 cleavage (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of Slit2C distribution from dual-tagged construct versus isolated fragment expression.

claim: Slit2C-GFP isolated fragment is more prone to deposition along the FP basal membrane than Slit2C processing product.
source: Furthermore, Slit2C-GFP isolated fragment was more prone to deposition along the FP basal membrane than Slit2C processing product (Figure 5K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative comparison of basal membrane deposition between isolated fragment and processing product.

claim: Slit2C and Slit2N distributions likely result from mechanisms regionalizing full-length Slit2 protein and its processing within the FP glial cell compartments.
source: Thus, Slit2C and Slit2N distributions likely result from mechanisms regionalizing full-length Slit2 protein and its processing within the FP glial cell compartments.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed differences in distribution patterns between processing products and isolated fragments.

claim: Preventing Slit2 cleavage results in strong depletion of Slit2 fluorescent signal in the basal compartment where commissural axons navigate.
source: Notably, preventing Slit2 cleavage resulted in strong depletion of Slit2 fluorescent signal in the basal compartment in which commissural axons navigate (Figure 6B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of dual-tagged Slit2-FL and Slit2-FL Δ (uncleavable) distribution in electroporated chicken embryos.

claim: Slit2-FL is not addressed to the basal processes but rather distributed in the apical compartment of FP glia cells where it is locally processed.
source: This suggested that Slit2-FL is not addressed to the basal processes, rather distributed in the apical compartment of FP glia cells, where it is locally processed, generating fragments that are subsequently deposited on the basal processes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that preventing cleavage depletes Slit2 from the basal compartment.

claim: The cleavage is determinant for proper localization of Slit2 fragments to the axon navigation path.
source: This confirmed that the cleavage is determinant for proper localization of Slit2 fragments to the axon navigation path.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that preventing cleavage results in depletion of Slit2 from the basal compartment.

claim: PC2 is a proprotein convertase involved in the activation of endocrine peptides.
source: Amontillado homolog in vertebrates is PC2, a proprotein convertase involved in the activation of endocrine peptides (Smeekens et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PC2 function and cites a previous publication (Smeekens et al., 1991).

claim: Treatment with CMK (PC2 inhibitor) results in loss of Slit2C-Venus fragment and accumulation of the FL form in N2a cells.
source: We treated N2a cells transfected with dual-tagged Slit2-FL with chloromethylketone (CMK), a PC2 inhibitor, and found that it resulted in a loss of the Slit2C-Venus fragment and an accumulation of the FL form, as observed with Slit2-FL Δ. (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot analysis of N2a cells treated with PC2 inhibitor.

claim: PC2 might either directly or indirectly be involved in Slit2 cleavage.
source: Thus, PC2 might either directly or indirectly be involved in Slit2 cleavage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PC2 inhibition affects Slit2 cleavage, but the mechanism is not definitively established.

claim: PC2 is mostly expressed in the FP.
source: We observed that PC2 was mostly expressed in the FP (Figure 6H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunolabeling of E4 chicken embryo transverse sections with anti-PC2 antibody.

claim: PC2 is enriched in the apical compartment with modest expression in the basal compartments of the FP.
source: Signal quantification revealed that PC2 is enriched in the apical compartment with modest expression in the basal compartments of the FP (Figure 6I and J).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of PC2 immunofluorescence signal in different FP compartments.

claim: CMK injection to chicken embryos electroporated with dual-tagged Slit2-FL results in significantly reduced basal/apical signal for both Slit2N and Slit2C compared to control.
source: By quantifying the distribution of Slit2N and Sit2C, we found in both cases that the basal/apical signal was significantly reduced in the CMK condition compared with the control, indicating decrease of fragments deposition in the axon navigation path (Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of Slit2 fragment distribution in CMK-treated versus control embryos.

claim: PC2 is expressed at an appropriate timing and location to mediate the cleavage of Slits and participate in setting their distribution patterns in the FP navigation path.
source: Thus overall, PC2 is expressed at an appropriate timing and location to mediate the cleavage of Slits and participate in the setting of their distribution patterns in the FP navigation path (Figure 6L).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of PC2 expression pattern and its effect on Slit2 cleavage and distribution.

claim: Much more complex pHluo-PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones (17%) were observed than pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ ones (5%).
source: We observed much more complex pHluo-PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones (17%) than pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ ones (5%) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of growth cone morphologies in electroporated chicken open-books.

claim: The capacity of SlitC to collapse PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F commissural growth cones was significantly reduced compared to that of Sema3B.
source: As expected from our previous overexpression experiments, the capacity of SlitC to collapse PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F commissural growth cones was significantly reduced, compared to that of Sema3B.
evidence: The claim is supported by collapse assay data on cultured PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F commissural neurons.

claim: In the SlitC/GDNF condition, PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F growth cones showed atypical shapes including long filopodia, contracted with numerous reminiscent filopodia, or visibly spread.
source: Interestingly, in the SlitC/GDNF condition, we noted growth cones with atypical shapes: long filopodia, or contracted with numerous reminiscent filopodia, or visibly spread (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphological observations of cultured PlxnA1Y1815F/Y1815F commissural neurons exposed to SlitC and GDNF.

claim: SlitC/PlxnA1 signaling might negatively regulate the complexity of growth cone morphologies.
source: This suggests that SlitC/PlxnA1 signaling might negatively regulate the complexity of growth cone morphologies.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PlxnA1Y1815F growth cones show increased morphological complexity.

claim: Much more exploratory behaviors were observed in the PlxnA1Y1815F+ population (59%) than in the pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ one (15%).
source: Strikingly, we observed much more exploratory behaviors in the PlxnA1Y1815F+ population (59%) than in the pHluo-PlxnA1WT+ one (15%) (Figure 7B and Videos 13–16).
evidence: The claim is supported by high-frequency time-lapse analysis of growth cone behaviors in chicken open-books.

claim: Split PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones were much more frequent (49%) than PlxnA1WT ones (9%).
source: While turned growth cones were found equally represented in both conditions, split PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones were much more frequent than PlxnA1WT ones (49% and 9% respectively) (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of growth cone behaviors in time-lapse sequences.

claim: Splitting is transient and followed by single growth cone reformation.
source: We did not observe collateral elongating from split growth cones, which suggests that splitting is transient and followed by single growth cone reformation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that no collaterals were observed elongating from split growth cones.

claim: Exploratory behaviors were present from the onset of FP navigation, not appearing after midline crossing or after FP exit.
source: Moreover, exploratory behaviors were not appearing after midline crossing or after FP exit, but were present from the onset of the FP navigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of growth cone behaviors during FP navigation.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones were significantly larger than PlxnA1WT+ ones.
source: We found that PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones were significantly larger than PlxnA1WT+ ones.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of growth cone width over time.

claim: PlxnA1Y1815F+ growth cones showed higher variations of width over time compared with PlxnA1WT+ growth cones.
source: In addition, their increased exploratory behavior was also reflected in the higher variations of width over time when compared with PlxnA1WT+ growth cones (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of growth cone width variations over time.

claim: SlitC does not act by pushing commissural axons after crossing but is deposited onto complex ramifications of FP glia basal process that mark out the entire FP navigation path.
source: Through combinations of in vivo analysis, live imaging, and super resolution microscopy, we show that SlitC does not act by pushing commissural axons after crossing. Instead, it is deposited onto remarkably complex ramifications of FP glia basal process that mark out the entire FP navigation path.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental approaches including imaging and functional analysis.

claim: Reiterated contacts with ligand-coated glial surfaces produce continuous constrains that protect growth cones from the risk of aberrant deviations.
source: Reiterated contacts with ligand-coated glial surfaces produce continuous constrains that protect the growth cones from the risk of aberrant deviations that could result from active exploration and response to other guidance cues of their local environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of FP glia architecture, ligand distribution, and growth cone behaviors.

claim: Rather than pushing growth cones and preventing them from turning back, SlitC constrains axon growth through aligned FP glia corridors, imposing continuous forward direction.
source: Thus, rather than pushing the growth cones and preventing them from turning back, SlitC constrains axon growth through aligned FP glia corridors, imposing them continuous forward direction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of FP architecture, ligand distribution, and functional analysis of PlxnA1Y1815F mutation.

claim: Spinal cord progenitors that synthesize Netrin1 use their basal process to redistribute Netrin at a more lateral position close to the basal lamina.
source: Recent work revealed that spinal cord progenitors that synthesize Netrin1, a major attractant for spinal cord commissural axons, take advantage of their basal process to redistribute Netrin at a more lateral position close to the basal lamina, where it promotes commissural axon navigation toward the FP (Varadarajan and Butler, 2017).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Varadarajan and Butler, 2017) to provide context.

claim: Early electronic microscopy images revealed close contacts between FP glia surfaces and axons and suggested complex shapes of basal processes.
source: Early electronic microscopy images revealed close contacts between FP glia surfaces and axons, and suggested complex shapes of basal processes (Yaginuma et al., 1991; Okabe et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim references previous publications (Yaginuma et al., 1991; Okabe et al., 2004) to provide historical context.

claim: Observations of FP cells in a β-galactosidase transgenic mouse line pointed out the complexity of basal processes.
source: Observations of FP cells in a β-galactosidase transgenic mouse line also pointed out the complexity of basal processes (Campbell and Peterson, 1993).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Campbell and Peterson, 1993) to provide context.

claim: Glia cells at the optic chiasm midline form a specific compartment, arranging a palisade that crossing retinal axons traverse.
source: In the developing brain, glia cells at the optic chiasm midline form a specific compartment, arranging a palisade that crossing retinal axons traverse (Marcus et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Marcus et al., 1995) to provide comparative context.

claim: The path of callosal axons across the midline is paved by radial glia processes.
source: The path of callosal axons across the midline is also paved by radial glia processes (Norris and Kalil, 1991).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Norris and Kalil, 1991) to provide comparative context.

claim: A radial glia scaffold lying at the frontier between the striatum and the globus pallidum guides corticospinal axons.
source: More recently, a radial glia scaffold lying at the frontier between the striatum and the globus pallidum was discovered to guide corticospinal axons (Kaur et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim references a recent publication (Kaur et al., 2020) to provide comparative context.

claim: Slit2C and Slit2N form distinct clusters in the FP.
source: Notably, we found that Slit2C, Slit2N, and Sema3B are prominently deposited in columnar patches covering the ramified basal processes of FP glia cells, with Slit2C and Slit2N forming distinct clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of dual-tagged Slit2 distribution in electroporated chicken embryos.

claim: Unlike in Drosophila midline guidance, FL-Slits likely play limited guidance role for commissural axons in vertebrates.
source: Thus, unlike in Drosophila midline guidance for which Slit processing was reported to be dispensable (Coleman et al., 2010), FL-Slits likely play limited guidance role for commissural axons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Slit2-FL concentrates in the soma and its cleavage is required for deposition in the axon path, and contrasts with findings in Drosophila (Coleman et al., 2010).

claim: The process of muscle anchorage to tendons in Drosophila requires Slit processing for proper distribution of fragments and functional outcome.
source: This is also consistent with previous studies of the process of muscle anchorage to tendons in Drosophila that reported the importance of Slit processing for subsequent distribution of the fragments and proper functional outcome (Ordan and Volk, 2016).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Ordan and Volk, 2016) to provide comparative context.

claim: SlitN and SlitC fragments have different cell association properties.
source: SlitN and SlitC fragments were reported to have different cell association properties (Brose et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Brose et al., 1999) to provide context.

claim: In zebrafish developing brain, apical end feet of radial glial cells organize through collagen IV the lamination of the neuropil by exposing Slits and heparan sulfate proteoglycans to axon terminals.
source: Interestingly, in the zebrafish developing brain, apical end feet of radial glial cells extend at the surface of the tectum, organizing through collagen IV the lamination of the neuropil by exposing Slits and heparan sulfate proteoglycans to axon terminals (Xiao et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Xiao et al., 2011) to provide comparative context.

claim: Morphogenesis of the Drosophila heart tube lumen relies on polarized localization of collagen XV/XVIII orthologue Multi-Plexin forming a macro-complex with Slit.
source: Morphogenesis of the Drosophila heart tube lumen was found to rely on polarized localization of the collagen XV/XVIII orthologue Multi-Plexin forming a macro-complex with Slit (Harpaz et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Harpaz et al., 2013) to provide comparative context.

claim: Loss of Syndecan results in modification of Slit distribution and activity in Drosophila.
source: In the context of midline crossing, loss of the heparan sulfate carrier (heparan sulfate proteoglycan) Syndecan results in modification of Slit distribution and activity in Drosophila (Johnson et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Johnson et al., 2004) to provide comparative context.

claim: Dystroglycan localizes Slit proteins in the basal lamina through non-cell autonomous action in the vertebrate spinal cord.
source: In the vertebrate spinal cord, dystroglycan was identified as a Slit binding partner, localizing the proteins in the basal lamina through non-cell autonomous action (Wright et al., 2012; Lindenmaier et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references previous publications (Wright et al., 2012; Lindenmaier et al., 2019) to provide context.

claim: Proteolysis of F-spondin generates two fragments, one of which is deposited at the basement membrane.
source: For example, proteolysis of the extracellular matrix protein F-spondin, reported to contribute to commissural axon guidance (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 1999), was found to generate two fragments, among which one is deposited at the basement membrane (Zisman et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim references previous publications (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 1999; Zisman et al., 2007) to provide comparative context.

claim: Proper FP crossing is thought to rely on a balance of positive and negative forces that support growth cone attachment, motility, and direction.
source: Proper FP crossing is thought to rely on a balance of positive and negative forces that support growth cone attachment, motility, and direction (Stoeckli et al., 1997; Fitzli et al., 2000; Gore et al., 2008; de Ramon Francàs et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim references previous publications to describe the current understanding of FP crossing mechanisms.

claim: Differential pre- and post-crossing sensitivities were reported in numerous experimental paradigms.
source: Consistently, differential pre- and post-crossing sensitivities were reported in numerous experimental paradigms (Zou et al., 2000; Delloye-Bourgeois et al., 2015; Nawabi et al., 2010) but such pushing action of the cues has not been clearly established.
evidence: The claim references previous publications (Zou et al., 2000; Delloye-Bourgeois et al., 2015; Nawabi et al., 2010) to provide context.

claim: SlitC acts by restricting the exploratory capacity of commissural growth cones which sort PlxnA1 when they enter the FP.
source: With our analysis of PlxnA1Y1815F model and live imaging paradigms, we show that SlitC acts by restricting the exploratory capacity of commissural growth cones, which sort PlxnA1 when they enter the FP (Pignata et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by functional analysis of PlxnA1Y1815F mutation and references previous work (Pignata et al., 2019) on PlxnA1 sorting.

claim: SlitC mode of action restricts the formation or stabilization of peripheral growth cone protrusions to constrain them in a non-exploratory state, favoring forward growth direction.
source: This function is served by the particular morphology of the FP glia cells that might impose repeated contacts of the growth cones with spots of ligands spanning the navigation path. Our functional analyses are all consistent with SlitC mode of action restricting the formation or the stabilization of peripheral growth cone protrusions to constrain them in a non-exploratory state, thus favoring forward growth direction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of FP architecture, ligand distribution, and growth cone behaviors in WT versus PlxnA1Y1815F conditions.

claim: Axons challenged to grow on micropatterned surfaces with uniform Sema3F substrate interrupted by permissive dots can efficiently extend with straight trajectories by jumping from one permissive dot to the next.
source: In recent work, axon growth was modeled using microcontact printing culture devices developed to examine individual growth cone responses to dots of guidance molecules (Ryu et al., 2019). Axons were challenged to grow on micropatterned surfaces consisting in uniform Sema3F substrate interrupted by permissive dots. They were found able to efficiently extend in such surfaces, having, in addition, a straight trajectory resulting from jumping from one permissive dot to the next one.
evidence: The claim references a recent publication (Ryu et al., 2019) to provide comparative context.

claim: Perturbing the distance between dots or their size on micropatterned surfaces modifies axon shape by disorganizing their cytoskeleton and trajectory, inducing curved growth patterns.
source: Interestingly, perturbing the distance between dots or their size modified the shape of the axons by disorganizing their cytoskeleton and their trajectory, inducing curved growth patterns (Ryu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references a recent publication (Ryu et al., 2019) to provide comparative context.

claim: A 'salt and pepper' context with repulsive ligands localized in spots intercalated with permissive regions might build an appropriate topographic environment for limiting growth deviations.
source: Thus, a 'salt and pepper' context as in the FP with repulsive ligands localized in spots and intercalated with permissive regions might build an appropriate topographic environment for limiting the possibilities of growth deviations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison with micropatterned surface experiments and the observed FP ligand distribution.

claim: Constraining growth cone exploration might be required for counteracting other local coincident guidance forces that would disturb axon trajectories during FP crossing.
source: Such constrain of growth cone exploration might also be required for counteracting other local coincident guidance forces that would disturb axon trajectories during FP crossing.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the functional significance of SlitC-mediated constrains.

claim: Growth cone exploration increases when they start navigating the second FP half, although they still keep a clear straight growth.
source: In our recent work, we found in live imaging that the exploration is increased when growth cones start navigating the second FP half, although we observed they still keep a clear straight growth (Pignata et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references previous work (Pignata et al., 2019) to provide context.

claim: Increased exploratory behavior in the second FP half could reflect increasing sensitivity to FP-derived Shh and Wnt rostro-caudal gradients that drive longitudinal turning after crossing.
source: This exploratory behavior could reflect an increasing sensitivity to FP-derived Shh and Wnt rostro-caudal gradients that were found to drive the longitudinal turning after the crossing (Zuñiga and Stoeckli, 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning that references previous work (Zuñiga and Stoeckli, 2017) on Shh and Wnt gradients.

claim: In Robo3 knockout embryos, commissural axons totally fail to cross the FP but turn longitudinally in the ipsilateral side.
source: In Robo3 knockout embryos, commissural axons totally fail to cross the FP but turn longitudinally in the ipsilateral side.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Robo3 knockout phenotypes.

claim: Non-crossing commissural axons can get sensitized to longitudinal gradients, reflecting the need for guidance constrains to counteract premature turning during FP navigation.
source: This argues that non-crossing commissural axons can get sensitized to longitudinal gradients, which also reflects the need for guidance constrains to counteract premature turning during the FP navigation (Friocourt and Chédotal, 2017).
evidence: The claim is inferred from Robo3 knockout phenotypes and references a previous publication (Friocourt and Chédotal, 2017).

claim: One function of PlxnA1/SlitC signaling is to prevent premature longitudinal turning until FP exit.
source: One function of PlxnA1/SlitC signaling would thus be to prevent premature longitudinal turning until FP exit.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PlxnA1Y1815F axons show increased premature turning.

claim: Despite early sensitivity to Slit fragments, commissural axons are still able to enter the FP, which might result from discrete spot distribution of cues on glial surfaces rather than diffuse distribution.
source: Our model supports that despite their early sensitivity to Slit fragments, commissural axons are still able to enter the FP. This might result from the distribution of the cues concentrating them in discrete spots deposited on the glial surfaces forming the corridors, rather than in diffuse distribution in the environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed ligand distribution patterns and axon behaviors.

claim: Signaling locally promoting axon entry into the FP could be concomitantly provided by FP cells, for example involving cell adhesion molecules.
source: Moreover, signaling locally promoting the entry of the axons could be concomitantly provided by FP cells, for example involving cell adhesion molecules, as reported in previous work (Stoeckli et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning that references previous work (Stoeckli et al., 1997) on cell adhesion molecules.

claim: Mutating Y1815 residue strongly impacts the distribution of PlxnA1 at the cell membrane.
source: The present study shows that mutating the Y1815 residue strongly impacts on the distribution of PlxnA1 at the cell membrane.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple observations of PlxnA1Y1815F distribution in different experimental paradigms.

claim: Y1815 could be required for allowing the formation of macro-complexes of PlxnAs at the growth cone membrane.
source: Structural analysis established the ability of PlxnA1 to engage its extracellular domain in dimeric complexes (Janssen et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2016). Thus, Y1815 could be required for allowing the formation of macro-complexes of PlxnAs at the growth cone membrane.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on structural studies (Janssen et al., 2010; Kong et al., 2016) and current findings.

claim: In astray mutation affecting Robo2 in zebrafish, retinal growth cones coursing toward and away from the midline are larger and less streamlined than WT ones, abnormally deviating their trajectory.
source: Interestingly, astray mutation in the zebrafish affecting the Robo2 gene was found to result in altered behaviors of navigating retinal axons, resembling those we report here for spinal commissural axons defective for PlxnA1-SlitC signaling. In astray mutants, retinal growth cones coursing toward the midline and away after crossing are larger and less streamlined than WT ones, also abnormally deviating their trajectory and not correcting their errors as WT ones do.
evidence: The claim provides comparative context from zebrafish studies to support the generality of the findings.

claim: In astray mutants, Slit patterns indicate these ligands flank the path, suggesting they act by channeling the growth of retinal axons in the ventral telencephalon.
source: Analysis of Slit patterns indicated that these ligands flank the path, suggesting they act by channeling the growth of retinal axons in the ventral telencephalon (Hutson and Chien, 2002).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Hutson and Chien, 2002) to provide comparative context.

claim: Recrossing phenotypes have been observed when PlxnA1 and Slit1-3, but not Robo1/2 or Sema3B, are inactivated in the mouse spinal cord.
source: In the mouse spinal cord, recrossing phenotypes have been observed when PlxnA1 and Slit1-3, but not Robo1/2 or Sema3B, are inactivated and we show here that it is manifested when PlxnA1 fails to properly mediate SlitC activity.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge from genetic studies and current findings.

claim: The lack of recrossing in Robo1/2 loss could be due to the specific temporal and spatial pattern of Robo1 receptor at the growth cone surface.
source: The lack of recrossing in context of Robo1/2 loss could be due to the specific temporal and spatial pattern of Robo1 receptor at the growth cone surface.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on previous findings about Robo1 sorting patterns.

claim: Growth cones navigating the first FP half express PlxnA1 but not yet Robo1, while in the second FP half they express both.
source: According to our previous work (Pignata et al., 2019), growth cones navigating the first FP half express PlxnA1 but not yet Robo1, while in the second FP half, they express both.
evidence: The claim references previous work (Pignata et al., 2019) to provide context.

claim: Robo2 is sorted only during post-crossing longitudinal navigation.
source: Robo2 was found to be sorted only during the post-crossing longitudinal navigation (Pignata et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim references previous work (Pignata et al., 2019) to provide context.

claim: In Robo1/2-/- embryos, cases of commissural axons aberrantly oriented within the FP were reported that could reflect alleviation of straight growth constrains.
source: Interestingly in Robo1/2-/- embryos, cases of commissural axons aberrantly oriented within the FP were reported that could reflect alleviation of straight growth constrains (Long et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim references a previous publication (Long et al., 2004) to provide comparative context.

claim: Continuously limiting growth cone exploration through short-range signaling that maintains straight trajectory can efficiently counteract coincident guidance cues destined for the next step, preventing premature directional changes until intermediate target navigation is completed.
source: Overall, our study raises a guidance model of midline crossing that might represent a general mechanism for the navigation at choice points. Continuously limiting growth cone exploration through short-range signaling that maintains their trajectory straight can efficiently counteract coincident guidance cues destined for the next step, preventing them to induce premature directional changes until intermediate target navigation is completed.
evidence: The claim is a general model inferred from the combined findings of the study.

claim: PC2 proprotein convertase activity contributes to the pattern of Slit ligands in the FP.
source: We found that PC2 proprotein convertase activity contributes to this pattern of ligands.
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing PC2 expression, its ability to cleave Slit2, and effects of PC2 inhibition on Slit fragment distribution.

claim: SlitC acting via PlexinA1 receptor is shared with another FP repellent, Semaphorin3B.
source: Next, we studied Slit-C acting via PlexinA1 receptor shared with another FP repellent, the Semaphorin3B, through generation of a mouse model baring PlexinA1Y1815F mutation abrogating SlitC but not Sema3B responsiveness, manipulations in the chicken embryo, and ex vivo live imaging.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PlexinA1 receptor function and is supported by experimental validation.

claim: PlexinA1Y1815F mutation abrogates SlitC but not Sema3B responsiveness.
source: Next, we studied Slit-C acting via PlexinA1 receptor shared with another FP repellent, the Semaphorin3B, through generation of a mouse model baring PlexinA1Y1815F mutation abrogating SlitC but not Sema3B responsiveness, manipulations in the chicken embryo, and ex vivo live imaging.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assays showing differential effects on SlitC versus Sema3B responses.

claim: SlitC constantly limits growth cone exploration, imposing ordered and forward-directed progression through aligned corridors formed by FP basal ramifications.
source: This revealed a guidance mechanism by which SlitC constantly limits growth cone exploration, imposing ordered and forward-directed progression through aligned corridors formed by FP basal ramifications.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion inferred from the combined findings of the study.
